extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians, postdocs, and advanced graduate students working on open problems or writing proofs
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for evaluating and validating mathematical research ideas and proofs, especially when working on difficult or unfamiliar open problems. Emphasises sceptical checks, counterexamples, stress-testing arguments, and an iterative model-case-driven development of methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be sceptical when a solution seems effortless
rubrics_metrics.description: If you unexpectedly find a problem solving itself almost effortlessly, and you can’t quite see why, you should try to analyse your solution more sceptically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether the method can also prove much stronger statements which are known to be false; such a phenomenon indicates a flaw. Treat surprisingly easy solutions as a warning sign and scrutinise them carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Try to look for counterexamples first
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are trying to prove some ambitious claim, you might try to first look for a counterexample; either you find one, which saves you time (and may be publishable), or you encounter an obstruction which gives a clue about what must be overcome to prove the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Searching for counterexamples both saves effort and 'identifies the enemy' that must be neutralised in a correct proof; use counterexamples to guide method development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply scepticism to others' claims to understand their strength
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply this type of scepticism to other mathematician’s claims also; it gives a sense of why the claim is true and how powerful it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use critical analysis of others' proofs to learn what parts are essential and how robust the argument is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce greater scepticism for famous/difficult or out-of-area problems
rubrics_metrics.description: A sceptical attitude towards your own work should be especially enforced when dealing with a problem which is known to be difficult (and this includes most 'famous problems'), or one which is outside your usual area of expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be especially wary of hand-waving and of steps where difficulty suddenly drops; write informal arguments out in full and seek external checks for unfamiliar techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for suspicious chains of transformations that suddenly simplify
rubrics_metrics.description: If your solution resembles repeated transforms of the problem with a sudden dramatic simplification (Transform ... Transform ... Suddenly the problem becomes much simpler! ... Solve the last simple problem. Done!), there is almost certainly a major error in the argument at the step where the simplification occurs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoroughly check and recheck the suspicious step, convert any hand-waving there into full written arguments, and analyse exactly what was the decisive step and why it could be so powerful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stress-test reductio ad absurdum arguments by removing the negation
rubrics_metrics.description: When using reductio ad absurdum with many computations that end in a contradiction, a good stress-test is to try to run the same argument without the initial assumption that the statement is false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the argument (perhaps with minor modifications) still yields a contradiction, the contradiction arises from the method, not from the negated hypothesis. Also try to untangle a reductio into a direct proof; this can both simplify the argument and expose errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware computations drifting away from the core subject of the conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: A warning sign is if the computations lead you further and further away from the mathematical topics and connections that the conjecture is supposed to be addressing (e.g. a purported proof of the Riemann hypothesis that uses meromorphic functions with almost no reference to integers or primes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that your methods actually engage the essential structures of the problem rather than detours that avoid the true heart of the matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be highly sceptical of a novel 'twist' on well-used methods
rubrics_metrics.description: If your approach adapts a method used frequently by many experts with an additional twist that all previous experts somehow 'missed', there is a high probability that this twist contains a serious technical flaw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give especially rigorous scrutiny to the new ingredient; previous experts may have avoided that route for substantive reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolate and solve toy/model cases first
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolate a toy model case x of major problem X and solve the model case using method A before attempting the full problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use toy problems to test methods, gain intuition, and identify properties that methods exploit; published partial results on model cases are valuable indicators of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use iterative extension from model cases to full problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Try using a method to solve more model cases; when it fails, identify what property P the method relies upon and test whether P holds more generally; conjecture P for all instances of X and then search for counterexamples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The path to a full solution is typically incremental: extend methods to more cases, formulate properties suggested by successes, and refine or abandon methods when counterexamples are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use counterexamples to refine or discard methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovering counterexamples to conjectured properties shows that either the current method must be adapted to avoid reliance on that property, or a new method is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take the simplest counterexample and study it deeply; try to prove the conjecture for that special case and see how methods fail or might be adapted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look to related problems and literature; consult experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Realise that a special case may be related to a problem z in another field; look up the literature on z and ask experts in that field for perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-field analogies and prior work often provide methods (method B) that can be adapted to your problem; literature search and expert contact are essential steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop adapted methods, iterate, and accumulate a toolkit
rubrics_metrics.description: After adapting methods from other fields (B → B'), iterate the toy-case/extension procedure; over time one acquires an array of methods each with strengths and weaknesses and considerable intuition about their applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine and simplify methods, locate new model problems, and seek unified frameworks in which prior results become special cases; expect this to take years in hard problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce problems to key conjectures and focus on decisive special cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Boil the problem down to a key conjecture K which provides decisive input; work to introduce new methods to attack important special cases of K and then rapidly develop them to settle K, and hence the original problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduction to a clean central conjecture and concentrated attack on pivotal special cases is a common and effective strategy in major breakthroughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert hand-waving into full written arguments and debug intuition step-by-step
rubrics_metrics.description: Any hand-waving arguments near suspicious steps should be written out in full; if you think you have a new result, go back and debug your intuition at each step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rewriting and making arguments explicit often reveals errors; it is good practice to try to rewrite reductio proofs as direct ones when possible and to strike out 'particularly fine' passages during revision to check for false elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quantitative and corollary checks as measures of difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Heuristics for difficulty include: (1) slight perturbations of hypotheses yielding counterexamples imply delicate proofs are needed; (2) lower bounds on quantitative dependencies (e.g. tower-exponential bounds) rule out overly simple approaches; (3) if a claimed result would imply many independent nontrivial corollaries, a very short/simple proof is unlikely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these meta-checks to judge whether an approach is plausibly strong enough or suspiciously too simple for the problem's genuine difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search the literature thoroughly and use prior work as a reality check
rubrics_metrics.description: Before celebrating a purported solution, search prior literature to ensure the approach or an essential lemma is not already known (and perhaps already indicates difficulties).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include discovering earlier work (e.g. Fejes Toth's 1948 result) that shows an 'almost' solution was previously known, revealing that the current line may be a red herring. Lack of literature awareness is a common trap.
